overview:
Malawi is a long, thin landlocked country in southeastern Africa, about the size of Pennsylvania, lying along the western shore of Lake Malawi, which fills about a fifth of its territory. It borders Tanzania, Mozambique, and Zambia. The capital, Lilongwe, is a spread-out city in the center, while Blantyre in the south is the commercial hub. Malawians call their country the Warm Heart of Africa for the friendliness of its people.

About 21 million people live in Malawi, making it one of the most densely populated countries in Africa, and most of them farm small plots of corn, tobacco, tea, and sugarcane. English and Chewa, also called Chichewa, are the official languages, and Tumbuka, Yao, and others are spoken in different regions. Most Malawians are Christian, with a Muslim minority along the lake. Malawi is a presidential republic that has held multiparty elections since 1994. It is one of the world's poorest countries, but it is known for peace, having never fought a war with a neighbor.
landAndNature: Lake Malawi, also called Lake Nyasa, is the star: about 580 kilometers long and up to 700 meters deep, it is the third-largest lake in Africa and holds more species of fish than any other lake on Earth, over 1,000 kinds, most of them colorful cichlids found nowhere else. Its clear waters and sandy beaches look like an ocean shore. The Great Rift Valley that cradles the lake is walled by highlands: the Nyika Plateau in the north is a rolling grassland of orchids, zebras, and roan antelope, and Mount Mulanje in the south rises to 3,002 meters, the highest peak in south-central Africa. Liwonde National Park along the Shire River has elephants, hippos, and reintroduced lions and rhinos, and fish eagles cry over the water. Baobabs dot the hot lakeshore.
peopleAndCulture: The Chewa are the largest group, along with the Lomwe, Yao, Ngoni, and Tumbuka. Nsima, a thick corn porridge, is eaten with relish of beans, greens, or chambo, a lake fish grilled or fried. Malawi's most famous tradition is Gule Wamkulu, the great dance of the Chewa, performed by masked dancers representing spirits and animals; it is recognized by UNESCO. Vimbuza healing dances of the Tumbuka are also on the list. Music mixes drums, the one-stringed banjo, and modern gospel and reggae, and Lake of Stars is a well-known music festival on the beach. Soccer is the favorite sport, and netball is popular with women; the national netball team, the Queens, ranks among the world's best. Many villages gather under trees for meetings and storytelling.
history: Bantu-speaking farmers settled around the lake by the 1000s and formed the Maravi kingdom, whose name became Malawi, meaning flames, perhaps from the lake glittering at sunrise. In the 1800s Yao and Swahili traders carried enslaved people from the region to the coast, and the Scottish missionary David Livingstone reached the lake in 1859 and campaigned against the slave trade. Britain made the area the protectorate of Nyasaland in 1891. John Chilembwe led an uprising in 1915. Independence came on July 6, 1964 under Hastings Kamuzu Banda, who ruled as president for life for 30 years, banning long hair and bell-bottom trousers. A referendum in 1993 brought multiparty democracy. In 2020 Malawi's courts overturned a flawed election and ordered a rerun, a first in Africa.
funFacts: Lake Malawi holds more fish species than any other lake on Earth, and most live nowhere else.
In 2020 Malawi became the first African country whose courts annulled a presidential election and ordered a new vote.
Under President Banda, men with long hair and women in trousers could be turned away at the border.
A Malawian teenager, William Kamkwamba, built a windmill from scrap to power his village, a story told in a book and film.
Mount Mulanje's Sapitwa peak, whose name means don't go there, is the highest point in south-central Africa.
